title: Data quality, observability and contracts
summary: Quality dimensions, tests and monitors, data contracts enforced at the producer, lineage, and running data incidents against SLOs.

blocks.text: 33.1 Dimensions of data quality
"Bad data" is too vague to fix. Break quality into dimensions, each with its own checks and owners.

head: Dimension
Question
Example check
rows: No null `customer_id`; row count within expected range
`status` in an accepted set; amounts not negative
Sum of order lines equals order total; every FK has a parent
Revenue reconciles with the finance ledger within 0.1%

blocks.text: Accuracy is the hardest: it needs an external reference (a ledger, a source-system count). The others can be checked inside the platform.
33.2 Tests versus monitors
Two complementary approaches catch different failures.

head: Tests (assertions)
Monitors (observability)
rows: Known failure modes: nulls, duplicates, broken FKs
Unknown unknowns: volume drop, distribution shift, late data
Only checks what you thought of

blocks.title: Soda Core checks (SodaCL)
blocks.text:
checks for fct_orders:
  - row_count > 0
  - missing_count(customer_id) = 0
  - duplicate_count(order_id) = 0
  - invalid_count(status) = 0:
      valid values: [placed, paid, shipped, cancelled]
  - freshness(loaded_at) < 2h

The same rules can be dbt data tests or Great Expectations expectations. What matters is *where* they run: a blocking test before publishing a gold table stops bad data reaching consumers; a non-blocking warning just records it. Use blocking checks on contract-level guarantees and warnings on heuristics.
Use the write-audit-publish pattern: write to a staging location (an Iceberg branch, a dev schema), run checks, then publish atomically. Consumers never see a failed batch (chapter 23).
33.3 Freshness, volume, schema and anomaly detection

items: **Freshness**: compare `max(event_ts)` or the last successful load with an expectation. Distinguish *the pipeline ran* from *the data is recent*: a job can succeed on an empty extract.
**Volume**: row counts per partition against a baseline, for example the same weekday over the last 8 weeks. A 40% drop on a Tuesday is suspicious; on a public holiday it may be normal.
**Schema**: detect added, removed or retyped columns at ingestion. A source renaming `amount` to `amount_eur` should be caught in bronze, not discovered in a dashboard.
**Distribution**: null rate, distinct counts, mean and percentiles per column. Catches unit changes (cents to euros) that pass every rule-based test.

blocks.text: Anomaly detection usually starts simple: rolling mean and standard deviation, or seasonal baselines by weekday and hour. Sophisticated models help less than good context: suppress alerts during known backfills, and route each alert to the owning team.
An alert channel with 50 alerts a day trains everyone to ignore it. Start with a few high-value monitors on gold tables, measure precision (alerts that led to action), and only then widen coverage.
33.4 Data contracts

A data contract is an agreement between a producer and its consumers about a dataset: **schema** (columns, types, nullability), **semantics** (what a field means, units, allowed values), and **service levels** (freshness, availability, support). The key idea is *enforcement at the producer*: a breaking change fails the producer's CI or deployment, instead of failing a dashboard three teams downstream.

blocks.title: dbt model contract (schema part)
blocks.text:
models:
  - name: dim_customers
    config:
      contract:
        enforced: true
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: number
        constraints:
          - type: not_null
      - name: country_code
        data_type: varchar
        description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, upper case

A dbt model contract fails the build if the model's output columns and types differ from the declaration. It covers schema; semantics and SLAs need tests, documentation and monitoring. For events, a schema registry with compatibility rules (for example backward compatibility for Avro or Protobuf) plays the same role (chapter 18). Open specifications for full contracts exist; check their current documentation before adopting one.
33.5 Lineage and impact analysis

Lineage is the graph of which datasets and jobs produce which others, ideally at column level. It answers two operational questions: *what broke this?* (upstream root cause) and *what will this break?* (downstream impact). Sources of lineage include dbt manifests, SQL parsing, OpenLineage events from Spark and Airflow, and query history in the warehouse.

blocks.title: A silent unit change
blocks.text: A payments team changed `amount` from cents to euros in their service. Every test passed: no nulls, no duplicates, positive values. A distribution monitor flagged that the mean of `amount` in bronze dropped by about 100x.
items: Column-level lineage showed 14 downstream models and 3 dashboards affected, including the board revenue report.
The data platform team paused publication of the affected gold tables and annotated dashboards as stale.
The payments team added the field to their data contract with an explicit unit, so a future change fails their CI.

blocks.text: 33.6 Incidents and SLOs for data

Treat data incidents like service incidents. A **SLA** is a commitment to consumers; an **SLO** is the internal objective, measured by a **SLI**. Examples: *`fct_orders` for day D is available by 06:00 on 99% of days in a quarter*; *fewer than 0.1% of rows fail validity checks*.

items: **Detect**: a test, monitor or user report.
**Triage**: severity by impact on consumers, found through lineage.
**Contain**: stop publication, mark data as stale, communicate to consumers.
**Fix and backfill**: correct the cause, re-run affected partitions idempotently.
**Review**: blameless post-incident review, new test or contract clause so it cannot recur silently.

blocks.text: Error budgets work for data too: if freshness SLOs are met with margin, the team can take more risk with changes; if the budget is spent, reliability work comes first.

blocks.title: Quality plan for a revenue mart
blocks.text: A gold `fct_revenue_daily` feeds finance reporting. It draws on orders (CDC), refunds (daily file) and FX rates (API). Design the checks: which are blocking tests and which are monitors, where each runs (bronze, silver, gold), which contract clauses you ask producers to accept, and the SLO you would publish.
hints: Which checks need an external reference to prove accuracy?
What do consumers see while an incident is open?

items: Split quality into dimensions: completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy, timeliness.
Tests catch known failures; monitors catch unknown ones. Use both, blocking only on guarantees.
Freshness, volume, schema and distribution monitors cover most silent failures; tune before widening.
Data contracts define schema, semantics and SLAs and are enforced at the producer.
Lineage drives root cause and impact analysis; run incidents with SLOs and blameless reviews.

blocks.q: A source switches amounts from cents to euros. Nulls, uniqueness and range tests still pass. Which control is most likely to catch it?
options: A distribution monitor on the amount column
blocks.explain: Only the value distribution changed; a monitor on mean or percentiles sees a step change. The other checks verify properties that did not change.

blocks.q: What is the defining feature of a data contract compared with a downstream test?
options: It is checked by the BI tool
It is enforced at the producer, so breaking changes fail before publication
blocks.explain: Contracts shift detection left to the producer's CI or deployment. YAML is incidental; contracts cover schema, semantics and SLAs, not just freshness.

blocks.q: A pipeline succeeded but extracted zero rows because of an expired API token. Which check fails?
blocks.explain: Job success says nothing about data recency. A row-count baseline or a freshness check on max(event time) catches an empty load; schema and uniqueness tests pass on empty data.

blocks.q: In write-audit-publish, when do consumers see new data?
options: After checks pass and the data is atomically published
Only after a manual approval in the BI tool
blocks.explain: Data is written to an isolated location, audited, then published in one atomic step. Consumers never see a batch that failed its checks.
